# hq

[arc reference](../index.md) › [Products](../index.md#products) › **Product**

## Why it exists

```tagline
The record office. One inked logbook nobody can tear a page from, one clerk who holds the pen, a tray of
things waiting for your signature, and a morning sheet that says what happened yesterday.
```

# Start here

## In plain words

Think of arc as a small company whose staff are AI models. Many of them do work. Someone has to keep the
books, or nobody can say what really happened.

**hq is the record office.** It does not build anything. It remembers, and it asks you for decisions.

```panel big
- **The logbook** (the spine). Every fact arc records is one line in ink, added in order. Nobody edits an old line or tears out a page. A mistake is fixed by writing a new line that points at the old one.
- **The clerk with the pen** (`arc-event`). Nobody else may write in the book. Every fact goes to this one clerk, who checks it and then writes it.
- **The tray** (the inbox). Requests that need your signature wait here. Nothing is stored in the tray itself. It is worked out fresh from the book each time.
- **The morning sheet** (the brief). One page for one day, made only from the book.
- **The accountant** (the P&L). Adds up money from the book at the moment you ask. Keeps no second set of numbers.
- **The rota** (the jobs). Small chores that run on a timetable, such as sealing yesterday.
- **The door guard** (the policy). Decides what a session may do: refuse it, only write it down as a proposal, or let it go ahead.
- **The reception window** (`arc dash`). The browser app never opens the book. It asks the window, and the window reads for it.

Because there is only one book, every other part of arc can trust the same story.
```

### Why this needs to be a product at all

Without a record office, arc would be many people each remembering things their own way.

| What you lose | What it looks like when it bites | hq's answer |
|---|---|---|
| **One true story** | Two parts of arc disagree about whether something ever happened. | One book, one writer. A fact is checked, then written once. |
| **Knowing what waits for you** | A separate "to do" list goes stale or gets lost. | The tray is never stored. It is recomputed from the book every time. |
| **Trusting the money number** | A saved total and a corrected receipt quietly disagree. | The accountant derives the total on the spot and caches nothing. |
| **A rule that cannot be switched off** | A session with write access deletes the very rule that limits it. | A few files are never given out as a place to write, however high the permission. |

> The last row is easy to miss. A guard that can be talked into removing itself is not a guard.

## arc words → normal words

```lede
Ten pieces of arc jargon. Each is an ordinary office thing wearing a technical name.
```

```rosetta
spine | the logbook | one line per fact, in order, never edited
event / receipt | one entry in the logbook | says what happened, who did it and whether it worked
kind | the type of entry | a fixed list of allowed types; a new type needs a new decision record
idem | the "already logged this" fingerprint | the same fact twice is refused, not written twice
quarantine | the reject pile | an entry that failed its checks goes here instead of the book
day closed | sealing yesterday's page | after that, a correction goes on a later day
inbox | the tray of things waiting for your signature | approve or reject, with a reason
brief | the one-page morning read | built only from the book
P&L | profit and loss, counted honestly | worked out from receipts when asked
L2 / `arc dash` | the reception window | the one place the browser app reads and decides through
```

## How a job flows

```lede
A fact has a short road into the book. It is refused at three of the four stops, and once it is in ink it stays.
```

```flow
source: something happens
box: ① Sent to the clerk | arc-event
box: ② Checked | secrets, shape, open day
box*: ③ Written | one line, in ink
box: ④ Read | brief, inbox, P&L
labels: checked, accepted, read
out: a secret inside | refused, nothing written
out: wrong shape | into the reject pile
out: that day is sealed | correct it on a new day
out: same fact twice | refused
divider: 2 | free to refuse | in ink for good
note: Before the line is written the clerk can still say no. After it, the only fix is a new line.
caption: Figure 1 — from something happening to something recorded. | The dashed line marks where a fact stops being easy to take back.
```

## The stages, one by one

```lede
Each stage is written twice: first what it does in ordinary words, then what actually happens.
```

```steps
t: The clerk writes a fact
plain: Anything that happened is handed to the one clerk. In a normal working session a bad entry never stops the work. In automated checks it stops loudly.
d: `emit` takes a kind and a payload, scans for secrets, validates against a fixed schema, and appends one line. Hook mode always exits 0 and sends a bad entry to the reject pile. Strict mode exits 2 on the same bad entry.
f: `.claude/scripts/hq/arc-event.mjs`

t: The tray shows what waits for you
plain: A request for your signature is just another entry. The tray finds the ones with no answer yet. You approve or reject, and give a reason.
d: `arc-inbox` folds each `decision.recorded` onto its `approval.requested` through the spine reader. It writes a decision only through the one writer, never straight into the files.
f: `.claude/scripts/hq/arc-inbox.mjs`

t: The morning sheet
plain: One page for one day, in the same order every time. Ask for the same day twice and you get the same page.
d: `arc-brief --date YYYY-MM-DD` renders the day from the spine reader. Output is deterministic, so it can be compared byte for byte after a rebuild.
f: `.claude/scripts/hq/arc-brief.mjs`

t: The accountant adds it up
plain: Money is counted from receipts at the moment you ask. At month end the totals must match the payment provider before the month can be closed.
d: `arc-pnl` derives the P&L on each run and stores nothing. Closing a month is blocked until the spine and the provider totals agree.
f: `.claude/scripts/hq/arc-pnl.mjs`

t: The rota runs the chores
plain: Chores run on a timetable, and a person running one by hand goes through the same door as the timetable.
d: `arc-jobs` walks four steps in one fixed order: lock, guards, execute, receipt. A scheduled run and a manual run differ only in who is named on the receipt. Cadences are `daily@HH:MM` or `weekdays@HH:MM`.
f: `.claude/scripts/hq/arc-jobs.mjs`

t: The door guard decides
plain: Before a session does something, the guard answers with one of three words. Not allowed. Allowed only as a written proposal. Or go ahead.
d: `policy-hook` reads the tool call, asks the one shared decision function, and answers in exit codes. Exit 2 means denied. The rulebook is `hq.policy.yaml`.
f: `.claude/scripts/hq/policy-hook.mjs`

t: The window serves the browser
plain: The browser app never touches the book. It asks the reception window to read, and the window is also the one place a decision from the app gets written.
d: `arc dash` binds to the local machine only, serves reads through the spine reader, and writes a decision through the same path as the command line.
f: `.claude/scripts/hq/arc-dash.mjs`
```

# The bigger loop

## A day, told as a story

This is an illustration, not a record of a real day.

Overnight the rota seals yesterday's page (the `day-close-roll` chore) and makes this morning's sheet (the `brief-materialize` chore). You open the app. The window
reads the book and shows the sheet. In the tray there is one request. You approve it and type a reason.
That approval becomes a new line in the book, the same line you would get from the command line. During
the day other parts of arc write their own facts through the clerk. Next month, before the books close,
the accountant checks the totals against the payment provider.

```loop
top: 1 | the request
top: 4 | the correction
stage: 1 · Requested | a line asks for your signature
stage: 2 · In the tray | worked out from the book
stage*: 3 · Decided | approve or reject, with a reason
stage: 4 · Written | a new line in ink
stage!: 5 · Later, a mistake | the day is already sealed
labels: waits, you decide, recorded, noticed
back: last -> 3 | a correction is a new line naming the old one
caption: Figure 2 — how a decision lives in the book. | The loop back is why nothing in the book is ever edited.
```

## Where the rules are written

- **One writer, one reader.** Only one script writes the book, and one reader is used to read it. A gate
  named `spine-api` checks that nothing else opens the raw log (ADR-0030).
- **A book of ink.** Append-only, with a fixed list of entry types (ADR-0024, ADR-0026).
- **Sealed days.** After a day is closed, a correction goes on a later day (ADR-0029).
- **Secrets never reach the book.** A secret found in an entry refuses it (ADR-0028).
- **Two modes.** The clerk never blocks a working session, and is strict in automated checks (ADR-0031).
- **Money is derived.** The ledger is a reader, and closing a month is a blocking check (ADR-1000,
  ADR-1005).
- **Un-grantable files.** A few files can never be given out as a place to write (ADR-0502).
- **One read door.** The browser app talks to the window, and a decision has one write path
  (ADR-1301, ADR-1302).
- **Two doors for work.** A short job is planned first and applied second, and what you read on the plan
  is exactly what runs (ADR-1326).

## Where hq sits in arc

- **Under a lot of arc.** It needs only `core`. Other products rely on hq for the book.
- **One command of its own.** `/arc-face-module` builds the four files for a room in the app and refuses a
  room the window does not serve.
- **Recording a decision.** The `adr-record` process writes one of your decisions down as a numbered decision record.
- **In the face.** hq has its own room, called spine. The chips at the top of this page name the room and
  the ring.

# Meta

## Glossary

```gloss
append-only: a record you can add to but never rewrite.
deterministic: the same input always gives the same output.
schema: the fixed shape an entry must have to be accepted.
reconcile: check that two sets of totals agree.
ledger: the list of money in and money out.
```
